San Francisco, California · ride

Bike routes in San Francisco

The rides locals in San Francisco actually do, each with a route you can load.

Best months: Any month.

More on when to ride

The Golden Gate Bridge is open to bikes every day of the year; in standard time, November to March, the west sidewalk runs a shorter clock (the bridge district’s page). The weekly rides in the directory run year-round. For Mt. Tamalpais, Jay’s Essential Bike Rides says to pick a day when the bay is clear of fog. The wind on Ridgecrest is strong.

Bike routes in San Francisco, listed

What do you need?

  1. Golden Gate Bridge and the Marin Headlands (Hawk Hill)

    Zone 1, the bridge ride.

    • Road
    • 28 mi
    • 2,400 ft up
    • Moderate
    • Start: Near the San Francisco Caltrain station
    • Water: Round House Café by the bridge Welcome Center; public restrooms at Vista Point, the north end of the bridge (Presidio Trust).
    • Watch: On the bridge you share a sidewalk with people walking.

    Ride it with the group: Fat Cake Tuesday Headlands and Arsicault (Tuesdays, 6:30 am); Hummingbird All Watts Welcome (intervals) (Tuesdays, 7:05 am) →

    Route on RideWithGPSRoute pageTo the start
    More about Golden Gate Bridge and the Marin Headlands (Hawk Hill)

    Out along the Embarcadero, across the Golden Gate Bridge, a clockwise lap of the Marin Headlands and back: 28 miles and about 2,400 feet, per the RideWithGPS page. The climb is Hawk Hill, Conzelman Road from the lot at the north end of the bridge: 1.8 miles and 538 feet at 5.8 percent (PJAMM). For the first day, the Presidio Trust publishes a short version: an 8-mile loop from Sports Basement at Crissy Field up to the bridge and Vista Point, back on the Bay Trail and the Presidio Promenade. Fat Cake’s Headlands and Arsicault ride (Tuesdays, 6:30 am) leaves the south end of the bridge and does this climb before the bakery. Hummingbird’s interval ride (Tuesdays, 7:05 am) does its efforts on Hawk Hill from the bridge Welcome Center.

    Surface: Paved: city streets and the Embarcadero, the bridge’s shared sidewalk, and the Headlands roads. About two-thirds of Hawk Hill has a bike lane (PJAMM).

    Watch: Which side bikes use changes by day, hour and season: on weekdays until 3:30 p.m. it is the east side; after that and on weekends, check the bridge’s own table. 15 mph on the sidewalk, 5 mph around the towers, and yield to people walking (Golden Gate Bridge district). Past the top of Hawk Hill, a rider’s review on PJAMM puts the drop on Conzelman at up to 18 percent.

  2. Sunset Dunes (the old Upper Great Highway)

    Zone 3, the easy one.

    • Path
    • 4 mi
    • Easy
    • Start: Lincoln Way entrance, the north end (or any cross street down to Sloat Blvd)
    • Water: Water fountains by the side path next to the restrooms at Judah and Taraval; restrooms at Sloat Blvd too, open during the day (the park’s own page).
    • Watch: The streets in from the Sunset (Kirkham, Ortega, Vicente, Sloat) are signed bike routes with no physical protection.

    Ride it with the group: Women and Non-Binary Bike SF Friday Morning Ride (2nd Friday and 4th Friday of the month, 7:15 am, departs 7:30 am) →

    Route pageTo the start
    More about Sunset Dunes (the old Upper Great Highway)

    The Upper Great Highway beside Ocean Beach, closed to cars and opened as a park, Sunset Dunes, in April 2025 (KQED). Two miles of old road by the sand; end to end and back is about 4 miles, the course the SF Bicycle Coalition used for its family ride. This is the ride for the evening you land: no cars, and you can turn around whenever you want. Women and Non-Binary Bike SF’s morning ride (2nd Friday and 4th Friday of the month, 7:15 am, departs 7:30 am) comes out here through Golden Gate Park’s car-free roads. Its future came up again in 2026. KQED reported (April 2026, updated September 2026) a citizen initiative gathering signatures for a measure to let cars back on weekdays. Whether it made a ballot was not confirmed when we checked, so read the park’s page before you plan around it.

    Surface: A former highway along Ocean Beach, closed to cars: 2 miles of old road (KQED), with entrances from Lincoln Way to Sloat Blvd (the park’s own page).

    Watch: Lincoln Way has a separated bike lane (the park’s own page). You share the park with people walking and skating.

  3. The Tiburon loop (Different Spokes’ Jersey Ride)

    • Road
    • 48 mi
    • 2,250 ft up
    • Hard
    • Start: Peet’s Coffee, 16th and Market, the Castro (the club’s ride page; check the club calendar), 2257 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94114
    • Water: Woodlands Market in Tiburon, the lunch stop on the club’s ride pages.

    Ride it with the group: Different Spokes Jersey Ride (2nd Saturday of the month, 8:45 am) →

    Route on RideWithGPSRoute pageTo the start
    More about The Tiburon loop (Different Spokes’ Jersey Ride)

    Zone 1 by way of the Castro: the route of Different Spokes’ Jersey Ride (2nd Saturday of the month, 8:45 am), the club ride of San Francisco’s LGBTQ+ cycling club. From the Castro across the Golden Gate Bridge to Sausalito, a small climb over Camino Alto, then out and around the Tiburon peninsula on Paradise Drive. 48 miles and 2,253 feet, per the club. Guests are welcome; there is no sweep, but the club regroups for slower riders. The Short and Sassy version, 24 miles and about 1,050 feet, leaves Mike’s Bikes in Sausalito, skips the bridge, and meets the long group for lunch in Tiburon. Woodlands Market was the lunch stop in May 2025. The club’s standing ride page puts the start at Peet’s on 16th and Market. Its August 2026 ride listing said Jane Warner Plaza, a block away at Castro and Market. Check the club calendar for the day’s start.

    Surface: Paved: city streets, the bridge’s shared sidewalk, Marin roads and the Corte Madera-Larkspur path (club pages).

    Watch: The bridge, which the club’s own page calls a mosh pit: you share the sidewalk with people walking, the side bikes use changes by day and hour, 15 mph on the sidewalk and 5 mph at the towers (Golden Gate Bridge district). The club cancels for heavy rain.

  4. Mt. Tam from Fairfax: Alpine Dam, the Seven Sisters and East Peak

    Zone 2, the climb.

    • Climb
    • 38 mi
    • 4,400 ft up
    • Hard
    • Start: The public lot in the median of Fairfax’s main street
    • Water: East Peak: restrooms, water and a visitor center (Jay’s page). Nothing between Alpine Dam and the top (PJAMM).
    • Watch: Broken pavement and launch ramps on the descents, and strong ocean wind along Ridgecrest (Jay’s page).
    Route pageTo the start
    More about Mt. Tam from Fairfax: Alpine Dam, the Seven Sisters and East Peak

    Jay’s Essential Bike Rides’ loop up Mt. Tamalpais. Fairfax-Bolinas Road over to Alpine Dam, then the climb past the dam to West Ridgecrest Boulevard and its 9 percent rollers, the Seven Sisters. A spur out to East Peak. Then down Pantoll Road and Panoramic Highway and back to Fairfax through Mill Valley, Larkspur, San Anselmo and Ross. 38 miles and 4,400 feet. The climb alone, Alpine Dam to West Peak, is 7.9 miles and 2,053 feet at 4.5 percent, 9.6 at its steepest (PJAMM). Splitrock Tap & Wheel, the bike shop and taproom on Sir Francis Drake in Fairfax, is where Marin Cyclists’ Point Reyes Station ride (Saturdays, 8:45 am) meets.

    Surface: Paved, with broken pavement in places (Jay’s Essential Bike Rides) and potholes on the first stretch of Fairfax-Bolinas Road (PJAMM).

    Watch: The same page says Fairfax-Bolinas Road is often under construction and signed closed; check before you go. It also says to wait for a day when the bay is clear of fog.

  5. San Francisco to Point Reyes Station

    Zone 2, the long day.

    • Road
    • 72 mi
    • 4,800 ft up
    • Hard
    • Start: San Francisco; the one-way version starts at Embarcadero BART
    • Watch: The route page says nothing about traffic or shoulders on Shoreline Highway or Highway 1.

    Ride it with the group: Marin Cyclists Fairfax to Point Reyes Station (Saturdays, 8:45 am) →

    Route on RideWithGPSTo the start
    More about San Francisco to Point Reyes Station

    Out to Sausalito and Mill Valley, Shoreline Highway over to Muir Beach and Stinson Beach, Highway 1 up to Olema and Point Reyes Station. Back by Nicasio, Fairfax, San Anselmo and Ross. 72 miles and about 4,800 feet, per the RideWithGPS page; its description stops after Ross, so check the last miles on the map. A one-way version, 70 miles and about 3,600 feet from Embarcadero BART, comes home on the Larkspur ferry (RideWithGPS). Bovine Bakery on Highway 1 in Point Reyes Station is the turnaround stop (see Coffee). Marin Cyclists’ ride from Fairfax to Point Reyes Station (Saturdays, 8:45 am) does the inland half with a group.

    Watch: On the bridge: shared sidewalk, the side bikes use changes by day and hour, 15 mph, 5 mph at the towers, yield to people walking (Golden Gate Bridge district).

  6. Marin Headlands dirt loop

    Zone 1, the gravel.

    • Gravel
    • 18 mi
    • 2,650 ft up
    • Hard
    • Start: Golden Gate Bridge plaza, San Francisco
    • Water: None named on the route page. It says to carry food and water.
    • Watch: Loose gravel in the turns on Bobcat Trail.
    Route on RideWithGPSRoute pageTo the start
    More about Marin Headlands dirt loop

    RideWithGPS’s ambassador route for the Headlands off the pavement: over the bridge, up Conzelman Road, then fire road and singletrack. The climbs are the Miwok Trail, at nearly 10 percent, and Marincello Road, a steady 9. The descents are technical singletrack on Old Springs Trail and the Coastal Trail. 18 miles and about 2,650 feet. Sports Basement in the Presidio and High Trails Cyclery on Polk Street rent a carbon gravel bike (see Bike shops).

    Surface: Mixed: pavement, fire road and singletrack. The page doesn’t give the dirt miles.

    Watch: Waterbars across lower Old Springs Trail; walk your bike through the Miwok Livery Stables; much of the loop has no phone signal (route page). On the bridge, 15 mph on the sidewalk, 5 mph at the towers, and yield to people walking (Golden Gate Bridge district).

  7. Old La Honda and Kings Mountain (Woodside)

    Zone 4, the Peninsula’s benchmark climb in a short loop.

    • Road
    • 19 mi
    • 2,600 ft up
    • Hard
    • Start: Woodside town center, the main intersection
    • Water: Alice’s Restaurant and a general store at Skyline and Route 84 (Bay Area Rides).
    • Watch: Kings Mountain Road is narrow and very twisty, and the descent is fast.
    Route on RideWithGPSRoute pageTo the start
    More about Old La Honda and Kings Mountain (Woodside)

    From Woodside by Whiskey Hill and Sand Hill roads to Old La Honda Road: almost exactly three miles at a touch under 8 percent, with short pitches up to about 14. North on Skyline, then down Kings Mountain Road. 19 miles and 2,600 feet (Bay Area Rides; the page dates from 2010). A 28-mile, 3,200-foot version from Menlo Park climbs Kings Mountain and comes down Old La Honda (RideWithGPS). Alice’s Restaurant at Skyline and 84 is the stop (see Restaurants). The Peninsula’s group rides are on this site’s Palo Alto hub, /rides/ca/palo-alto/, not re-listed here.

    Surface: Paved, narrow; the upper pavement on Old La Honda is bad (RideWithGPS note).

    Watch: Skyline has fast drivers and little shoulder. Old La Honda is very narrow, with bad pavement near the top (Bay Area Rides; RideWithGPS).

  8. Grizzly Peak and Redwood Road (Berkeley hills)

    Zone 5, the East Bay, a BART ride from the city.

    • Road
    • 44 mi
    • 4,500 ft up
    • Hard
    • Start: Spruce St and Grizzly Peak Blvd, Berkeley
    • Water: Restrooms and water at Sibley Volcanic Regional Preserve, on Skyline 100 feet south of the Grizzly Peak intersection (Jay’s page).
    • Watch: Traffic on the residential stretch of Grizzly Peak is dangerous.
    Route pageTo the start
    More about Grizzly Peak and Redwood Road (Berkeley hills)

    The hills loop from Jay’s Essential Bike Rides (updated September 2026): Grizzly Peak Boulevard along the ridge, Skyline, Pinehurst Road and Redwood Road, then down Claremont Avenue. About 44 miles and 4,510 feet. The Three Bears Loop, the other East Bay classic, is 38 miles and about 3,250 feet from Berkeley on its RideWithGPS page. Peet’s on Domingo, next to the Claremont Hotel (see Coffee), is the start of Berkeley Bicycle Club’s rides: Berkeley Bicycle Club Friday Coffee Ride (Fridays, 6:45 am); Berkeley Bicycle Club Sunday WTFN Ride (2nd Sunday of the month, 8:30 am).

    Surface: Paved; the corners on Pinehurst Road are often gravelly.

    Watch: Pinehurst’s corners are sharp and often gravelly; Claremont Avenue comes down at 10 percent for 2 miles, curvy and very fast (Jay’s page).
